why: The system had no way to reach the owner with the browser closed. Every notification
path ended either in a page nobody had open or in the fake push provider's in-memory
log, so 'the owner has been told' was true only while they were already looking.
A desktop toast is the one channel that works when the browser is shut and the screen
is locked, and it is the device's to raise: only the companion process runs in the
owner's interactive session. The Cloud Core cannot show a toast and must not pretend
to - it sends this shape and the device answers whether the toast was actually shown.
Written as a contract before either half was built, because the last four capabilities
that were not (file.search roots, the app manifest, the native manifest, the device
protocol schema) each shipped with both halves' suites green and neither half able to
talk to the other.

title.why: Windows truncates a toast title past roughly this; sending more is sending something the owner will not see.

body.why: Two lines of toast text. Longer belongs in the inbox, which already has the whole thing.

notification_id.why: The row in `notifications`. The device echoes it back so an action button can be attributed to the notification it came from, and so a repeat send is recognisable as the same notification rather than a second one.

priority.why: `urgent` asks Windows for a toast that stays on screen until dismissed; the others expire on their own.

group_key.why: Windows' own collapse key. Two notifications about one thing replace each other in the Action Center instead of stacking.

actions.why: Toast action buttons. Three is Windows' own limit; asking for more silently drops the extras, so the contract refuses them instead.

id.why: Echoed back verbatim when the owner presses it. A closed vocabulary the Cloud Core chose, never free text from a model.

label.why: What the button says, in Turkish. Windows gives a button about this much room.

shown.why: Whether a toast was actually raised. FALSE is a real answer - no interactive session, notifications disabled by the owner in Windows settings, or the shell not running - and the Cloud Core steps down its ladder rather than recording a delivery that did not happen.

reason.why: Which of them, because the owner's remedy differs: enable notifications, or log in.

notification_id.why: Echoed, so a late answer cannot be attributed to whichever notification is current.

surface.why: B11-toast: which surface carried it. 'toast' is a Windows toast under the companion's AppUserModelID, with the request's buttons; 'balloon' is the tray fallback used only when the toast platform cannot be used, and it has no buttons.

actions_rendered.why: How many of the request's buttons are on screen. Always 0 on a balloon, so a button the owner cannot press is never counted as offered.

notifier_setting.why: What Windows' ToastNotifier.Setting said. The three owner/machine choices (for_application, for_user, by_group_policy) answer shown:false with notifications_disabled - a balloon from the same process would route around them. 'unknown' means the platform could not be asked - including an id Windows holds no settings for yet, which is every id before its first toast (measured on Windows 10 19045); the toast is then tried and the history read-back decides.

user_state.why: The shell's SHQueryUserNotificationState when the toast was raised, when it could be read. A hint about whether a popup was likely to appear; Focus Assist is not reported by any public Windows API and is not claimed here.

detail.why: A short machine-readable note: why a fallback was used (app_identity_unavailable, toast_platform_unavailable, toast_show_failed, toast_not_in_history - Show returned but Windows' own notification history did not hold the toast), or actions_not_rendered on a balloon. Sent with shown true as well.

why: When the owner presses a toast button the device sends this as a device event, not as
a response: the toast may be pressed minutes after the command that raised it has
already been answered, and holding a command open for a human's attention span is how
a queue fills up.

payload.notification_id: uuid, the notification the toast belonged to
payload.action_id: the id of the pressed button, verbatim from the request

why: B11-toast: the payload objects ride in the heartbeat's optional status object, as the
list named by 'field' (DEVICE_PROTOCOL.md §6g, §6q) - the same place this device
already reports its own local alarm rings and snoozes. No new frame type, so an older
broker that does not know the field ignores it. A heartbeat is fire-and-forget, so each
press is carried in 'transmissions' consecutive reports and the Cloud Core records it
once, keyed on notification_id, action_id and pressed_at. The device accepts a press
only for a toast it showed and an action id that toast offered; the Cloud Core accepts
it only for an action its own row offered. A press is data: nothing on either side
runs, opens or launches anything because of it.

refused: a title or body over its limit (the device refuses rather than truncating - the Cloud Core should decide what the owner reads, not the toast layer)
a notification_id that is not a uuid
not_in_this_contract: Whether the owner READ it. A toast that appeared while nobody was at the desk was shown and not read; `read_at` belongs to the inbox and is set when the owner opens it.
Retrying. The Cloud Core's ladder decides what happens after `shown: false`; the device answers about one attempt and forgets it.
